title: Śrīdhara Svāmī literal English — Canto 4, chapter 1, first checkpoint
note: Only Śrīdhara Svāmī's own Sanskrit is rendered. His source groups 8–9, 18–20, 21–22 and 25–26. The source repeats its 4.1.31 heading for two different verses, so the rest of this chapter is withheld pending alignment; no later heading is silently trusted.

entries.text: Obeisance to Śrī Rāmacandra, whose lotus-foot nectar of consciousness is tasted by the supreme swans and who dwells in the minds of devotees. Now, in thirty-one chapters of the fourth [canto], secondary creation is declared. Secondary creation is brought about by Brahmā, the Manus and others who depend upon the Lord. In this first chapter the separate lineages of Manu's daughters are described, among which Hari appears in forms such as Yajña. To state Manu's daughters' lineage in detail, he says, ‘Of Manu, however.’ The word ‘and’ also indicates his two sons.

The word ‘however’ indicates that a son was also obtained by another means. To show this he says ‘adopting the putrikā-dharma’: the putrikā-dharma is the giving of a daughter under the verbal agreement, ‘I shall give you a daughter without a brother, adorned; the son born from her shall become my son.’ It is normally recognized in the case of a daughter without a brother and a man who desires a son. Nevertheless, desiring many sons, Manu did so even with a daughter who had brothers.
‘A pair’ means a male and a female. ‘By concentration’ means by meditation on the Lord.
Bhūti is Lakṣmī; she was a portion of Lakṣmī. Thus the marriage of the two is not incongruous: this is the sense.
The son of his daughter Ākūti was Yajña.
‘Lord of the yajus’ means Viṣṇu, the Lord of sacrifices or of their mantras.
‘Twice six’ means twelve.

Incidentally, with the two verses beginning ‘Tuṣitā,’ he states the group of six belonging to Svāyambhuva's manvantara. It will be said: ‘A manvantara is said to have six divisions: Manu, the gods, Manu's sons, the lord of the gods, the sages, and the partial descents of Hari’ [Bhāgavatam 12.7.15]. Here Svāyambhuva is Manu; the Tuṣitās are the gods; the seven seers are headed by Marīci; Yajña is Hari's descent, and he himself is Indra, lord of the divine host. Priyavrata and Uttānapāda are Manu's sons and rulers of the earth. Thus there are six divisions through the twofold role of Yajña. That manvantara was continued, pervaded and protected by the lineages of their sons, grandsons and further descendants.
‘Heard for the most part’ means heard extensively. ‘For the most part’ is used because the lineages of her daughters have not yet been heard.
‘The progeny of Prasūti’ means the expansion through sons, grandsons and so on.
The world was filled by the lineages of those two.

The lineage of Kaśyapa will be described in the sixth [canto]. He gives the lineage of the second with ‘Pūrṇimā.’ There was also a daughter named Devakulyā, who in another birth became Gaṅgā, the river of heaven, from the washing of Hari's feet.
‘Born of Self, Lord and Brahmā’ means born from portions of Viṣṇu, Rudra and Brahmā.
‘Something’ means ‘what exactly?’; that is, ‘What did they wish to do?’
[He went to] the ancestral mountain named Ṛkṣa, while established in austerity.
‘On that’ means on that ancestral mountain. The forest was of palāśa and aśoka trees bearing clusters of flowers. ‘Resounding’ means sounding with the flowing waters of the river named Nirvindhyā.

It was fire for which breath-control itself was the kindling, the igniting fuel; seeing the three worlds tormented by that fire issuing from the sage's head, the three lords went to his hermitage, as the next verse completes the construction. Their fame was being extended by the apsarases and those headed by them.
Their manifestation was their becoming visible; the conjunction with it was their nearness. His mind was illumined by it. ‘Rising’ means standing erect.

‘Offering’ means flowers and the like in his joined hands. ‘He attended upon them’ means he worshipped them. They were mounted on the bull and the other mounts. Their respective marks were the trident, water-pot, discus and the like.

Their gaze was one of compassion; by it and by their smiling faces they were made known as gracious. ‘By their radiance’ means by their brilliance [his eyes were overcome]. ‘Gentle’ means sweet; ‘well-spoken’ means bearing profound meaning.

‘In each age’ means in each kalpa. You are the well-known Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Giriśa, who have assumed bodies in their respective divisions. ‘I bow to you’ addresses you all. ‘From among you, which one was invoked by me?’ For he had specified one alone with ‘I take refuge in him.’ Which one of you is that one? You yourselves should say: this is the meaning.

This is elaborated by ‘One’: ‘by various principal offerings’; there is also the reading ‘O foremost of the gods.’ ‘For procreation’ means for the birth of a son. ‘Made into an object of thought’ means made one with the mind. How did all three of you come here, though you are beyond even the mind, beyond its reach?

As the resolve was made by you, so indeed must it come to pass, not otherwise, because your resolve is a true resolve. Then why did three appear when one was meditated upon? They say: ‘That one reality called the Lord of the world which you meditate upon—these are we.’ All three are that one reality itself; there is no difference among us: this is the meaning.
